mainText: Good morning, Zain. Today's biopharma news is split between a late-stage success for a psychedelic therapy, a safety warning on a rare disease drug, and a new immunology player raising capital. Definium Therapeutics reported its oral LSD candidate met the primary endpoint in the first of two phase three trials for generalized anxiety disorder, a milestone that could validate the company's platform and attract partnership interest. Meanwhile, a panel of experts flagged potential safety issues with Neurocrine's Vykat XR for Prader-Willi syndrome after seven reported deaths, prompting a call for tighter monitoring and possibly a regulatory review. In funding news, Boulevard Bio closed a sixty-five-million-dollar round to advance antibody candidates, including a deal to acquire Vera's IgAN program, positioning the startup to compete in autoimmune disease space. Also notable is Aureka Biotechnologies' one-hundred-million-dollar series B to build a biological world model for drug discovery, a move that could reshape how small biotechs approach target validation. The day also brings a second child death in a Chinese CRISPR trial, underscoring the risks of gene editing in pediatric patients and the scrutiny such programs now face. Worth reading deeper: the Endpoints feature on Definium's LSD trial details the design and what a positive read-out means for the broader psychedelic market, and why investors are watching the next phase closely. That's your rundown. Have a good one.

Good morning, Zain. Here's your biopharma rundown.

Let's start with the trial news, because there's a lot of it today, and not all of it is good.

Sionna Therapeutics had a rough one. Their experimental cystic fibrosis pill, which they were testing as an add-on to Vertex's blockbuster Trikafta, completely missed the mark in a Phase 2 trial. No benefit at all. The company is shelving the drug and hinting at layoffs while it "preserves capital." Wall Street didn't wait around — Sionna shed about two billion dollars in market value.

Tenax Therapeutics had it even worse. Their oral heart failure drug failed its pivotal Phase 3 study, showing no improvement in exercise capacity or symptoms versus placebo. There's no approved treatment for this specific condition, PH-HFpEF, so a lot of investors were banking on this one. The stock cratered eighty-four percent.

And in a genuine surprise, the FDA rejected a radiopharmaceutical from ITM — a therapy that was positioned to go head to head with a Novartis treatment. The agency cited manufacturing issues, not efficacy concerns, but it's still a real blow, especially since radiopharma has been getting a lot of hype lately. STAT has a broader piece today on how radiopharmaceuticals are running into unexpected toxicity problems — kidney, liver, and bone marrow issues — as more of these drugs move through trials. Worth keeping an eye on if you follow that space.

Now for the good news. AbCellera's stock jumped thirty-one percent after striking Phase 2 data — their drug cut hot flash frequency roughly in half for postmenopausal women. And Silence Therapeutics posted strong Phase 2 results for a gene-silencing drug in polycythemia vera, a rare blood cancer. Eighty-eight percent of patients responded, versus nineteen percent on placebo. That sets them up to compete with a Takeda drug that's already nearing approval.

On the deal front, Jazz Pharmaceuticals is doubling down on epilepsy, acquiring Actio Biosciences for eight hundred twenty million dollars upfront, plus up to five hundred million more in milestones, for an ultra-rare epilepsy program. On the funding side, Aureka Biotechnologies raised a hundred-million-dollar Series B to build what they're calling a biological world model for drug discovery, and a group of BioNTech veterans just landed twenty-five million in seed funding for a virtual cancer surveillance startup.

A few regulatory items worth knowing. Grail's Galleri cancer blood test is heading to an FDA advisory panel on September twenty-third — a big step toward the first approved multi-cancer early detection test. Though it comes with an asterisk: their landmark NHS trial missed its primary endpoint earlier this year, even though a subset of twelve cancers showed more encouraging results.

Separately, Sanofi is dealing with a shortage of two Pompe disease medicines after the FDA flagged manufacturing issues at their Irish plant. That one's worth watching if you have patients relying on Myozyme or Nexviazyme.

And China is tightening the rules around its investigator-initiated trials after some patient deaths and oversight concerns. That's the regulatory framework that's helped fuel a lot of China's biotech speed, so this could slow things down there.

One more on the policy side. The Trump administration issued a new executive order revisiting childhood vaccine policy, questioning the existing schedule. Worth watching given how politically charged that's been.

Worth reading deeper: the STAT piece on radiopharmaceutical toxicity. It ties together the ITM rejection and a broader pattern that's starting to show up across the field.

That's your rundown. Have a good one.
